claims.statement: Hebrews identifies Jesus as High Priest according to the order of Melchizedek.
Jeremiah announces a new covenant that is not like the covenant made at Sinai.
Psalm 110 addresses a figure who is declared a priest forever after the order of Melchizedek.
Genesis presents an unconditional promise to Abraham of descendants, land and blessing to the nations.
The Sinai covenant establishes a hereditary Levitical priesthood tied to sacrificial service.
Hebrews reads the silence of Genesis 14 about Melchizedek's genealogy as significant: "without father or mother… resembling the Son of God."
Hebrews argues that a change of priesthood necessarily entails a change of law.
The Melchizedekian priesthood of Christ supersedes the Levitical priesthood and its sacrificial order.

dependencies.rationale: Hebrews 5:6 and 7:17 quote Psalm 110:4 directly; the Melchizedekian title rests on the psalm.
Hebrews 7:11–16 argues by contrast with the hereditary Levitical order.
Hebrews 8:8–12 cites Jeremiah 31 to ground a change of covenant alongside the change of priesthood.
Jeremiah 31:32 defines the new covenant against the covenant made at Sinai.
Psalm 110 draws on Genesis 14, where Melchizedek blesses Abraham; reading the link as typology is interpretive.
The likeness of Melchizedek to "the Son of God" (7:3) is the bridge Hebrews uses to apply the order to Jesus.
The lemma presupposes that the Mosaic law is bound to the Levitical priesthood (7:11).
The supersession thesis requires that Jesus actually holds the Melchizedekian priesthood.
Without the priesthood-law linkage, a new priesthood would not displace the Levitical order.
Jeremiah's "not like the covenant" (31:32) supplies the covenantal frame Hebrews 8 builds on.

axioms.label: Apostolic exegesis is authoritative
axioms.statement: New Testament authors' readings of the Hebrew Bible are normative interpretations, not merely historical reception.
axioms.rationale: Grounds the use of Hebrews' reading of Psalm 110 and Genesis 14 as determinative of their meaning.

axioms.label: Figures prefigure fulfilment
axioms.statement: Persons, institutions and events in earlier scripture can foreshadow later realities beyond their authors' horizon.
axioms.rationale: Licenses reading Melchizedek and the Levitical cult as types of Christ.

axioms.label: One covenant of grace
axioms.statement: The biblical covenants are successive administrations of a single covenant of grace; the new covenant fulfils rather than cancels the old.
axioms.rationale: Frames the priesthood change as fulfilment within continuity.

axioms.label: Israel and the church remain distinct
axioms.statement: Promises made to national Israel retain literal force and are not absorbed by the church.
axioms.rationale: Qualifies supersession: Jeremiah's new covenant is addressed to Israel and Judah.

axioms.label: Torah is eternal and unabrogated
axioms.statement: The Written Torah, read through the Oral Torah, remains binding; no later revelation replaces it.
axioms.rationale: Rejects any change of law and reads Psalm 110 without priestly-messianic transfer.

axioms.label: Original context precedes reception
axioms.statement: A text's meaning is first established in its historical setting; later reuse is reception history, not the text's own sense.
axioms.rationale: Separates what Psalm 110 meant in its royal setting from Hebrews' later application.

claim_axioms.note: Descriptive claim about Hebrews; holds as a report of the text, but its theological force relies on apostolic authority.
Treating Genesis' silence as meaningful is a typological move.
The inference treats Hebrews' argument as normative.
Supersession reads the Levitical order as a shadow (Hebrews 8:5, 10:1).
Covenant theology frames supersession as fulfilment within one covenant of grace.
The psalm's royal-priestly figure is identified first in its Davidic setting.

counter_models.title: Torah permanence
counter_models.thesis: No priesthood change abrogates the Torah; the Levitical order is suspended by the Temple's loss, not superseded.
counter_models.alternative_reading: Psalm 110 addresses a Davidic king (or Abraham, in b. Nedarim 32b), whose priestly honour is not transferred to a later figure.

counter_models.title: Israel-specific new covenant
counter_models.thesis: The new covenant is addressed to Israel and Judah and its fulfilment for them is not exhausted by the church.
counter_models.alternative_reading: Hebrews applies Jeremiah to the church by extension; Israel's covenantal identity persists (Romans 11:29).

counter_models.title: Rhetorical silence
counter_models.thesis: Hebrews 7:3 uses a known exegetical convention (quod non in thora non in mundo); it makes no claim about Melchizedek's nature.
counter_models.alternative_reading: Read as Alexandrian-style argument from silence comparable to Philo, not as ontology.

counter_models.title: Royal, not messianic-priestly
counter_models.thesis: Psalm 110 is a royal enthronement psalm granting a Jerusalem king Melchizedek-like priestly prerogatives.
counter_models.alternative_reading: The "priest forever" grants dynastic cultic rights to the Davidic king rather than predicting a future figure.

map_links.note: Prophetic promise of a new covenant.
Priesthood bound to law and covenant.
Hebrews' reading of the new covenant as superseding the Levitical order.
